utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon -- good morning, everybody. I've been working already a few hours. That's the reason. So Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. Is there anyone else there? No. The Defence teams absentees are today Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Lazarevic, and Mr. Haynes. Mr. Obradovic, good morning to you. All right. It will soon be over. Mr. McCloskey is going to finish his cross-examination, and then we see if there is re-examination, and you can go home. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Cross-examination by Mr. McCloskey [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to go to the time-period when you got to Crna Rijeka on the 17th of July. From the 17th to, oh, roughly the first part of August, did you come to work every day at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My place of residence and work was there, and I didn't go elsewhere but to Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Basically, you stayed there the whole time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was General Miletic there doing the same thing with you, sleeping and working at Crna Rijeka that month of July after you got there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about General Milovanovic? We've seen on a film that he came to Zivanovic's going-away function out at the Jela Restaurant. I think it was on the 20th. Do you recall whether Milovanovic actually came to Crna Rijeka at all during July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that 20th of July -- excuse me. Before the -- before the departure of General Milovanovic at the Jela Restaurant, the referring was prepared, which was conducted by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- we got a translation of a word I don't quite understand. Can you describe to -- what it was that General Milovanovic did as translated to me as a "referring"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, he chaired the process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the process? What was this? Was it the morning staff meeting or something special?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The commander of the corps were informed that they had to come, or if they couldn't come that they had to send their deputies upon the departure -- to the departure of General Milovanovic, and they were instructed to prepare a briefing about the condition in their respective sector about the situation with the enemy and the enemy's intentions and the plans for the coming period. And before the ceremony began - at 10.00, I believe; I'm not sure - they started the briefing, and that briefing took place has Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just to try to understand this, did Milovanovic come by Crna Rijeka the morning of the 20th, the day of the party?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I'm sure that he was in charge of the briefing process. He chaired the briefing possess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the briefing process?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he must have been at Crna Rijeka that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at the briefing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the conversation with the corps commands and the members of the Main Staff that had taken part, I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Miletic, to your knowledge, at that morning briefing by Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a morning briefing. It was the briefing of the corps commands, the airforce, and anti-aircraft command -- sorry, anti-aircraft defence and the military schools, and General Milovanovic was present at that briefing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Miletic present?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So I said. General Miletic was present at that briefing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is a little problem with translations. We're all waking up, so bear with us. And I apologise. I now understand it, it wasn't a Milovanovic briefing; it was a briefing by the corps to the Main Staff, then, MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you learn what General Krstic had reported to the Main Staff about the situation he was facing in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not at that briefing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he at the party?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there. Because the Jela Motel is a good 10 kilometres away from Crna Rijeka, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We drove by there a couple of years ago, what's left of it. How long does it take to get from Crna Rijeka to the Jela Restaurant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20 minutes, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was General Mladic at the briefing by the corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not present because if he had been he would have been in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I can tell you, there was a film of that going-away function, and General Krstic was certainly there and gave a speech. So knowing that he was there at that time, does that help refresh your recollection as to whether he was at the -- the briefing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you specifically remember General Miletic telling you Krstic wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if General Miletic said so to me, but I don't think that Zivanovic was there either. So neither the commander nor the Chief of Staff was there, because at that time I don't know if Krstic had already been appointed commander, but neither Zivanovic nor Krstic were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Malcic was at the briefing, too, from the sector for organisation, mob [as interpreted], and personal affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he's the one that told you that Mladic -- sorry, that Zivanovic and Krstic were not at the morning briefing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I inquired about it, and we spoke about the persons who were present and how the briefing went, so that's how I learned about it. But I didn't ask specific questions about the presence of Generals Zivanovic or Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, where did you learn they were at that time when they didn't go to the briefing? I think when Milovanovic orders the presence of corps commanders, they generally show up or have a very good excuse.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was an order issued by the commander of the Main Staff, and I know that from the East Bosnian Corps the commander didn't come, but instead, his Chief of Staff, General Gabric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you learn where Krstic and Zivanovic were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask questions about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the going-away film, we see Mladic flying in in a little helicopter. Where he was he coming from, to your knowledge? You were -- you know, you were at the -- probably the ops room that day, and I'm sure at the ops room you keep track where -- well, you try to keep track where General Mladic is.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he had come from the area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what you know about that. What he had he been doing in Zepa that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what he was doing. I don't know. I wasn't with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Gvero at the briefing by the corps command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Aside from that briefing that you'd heard about that General Milovanovic led, were you aware of General Milovanovic coming to Crna Rijeka on any other day in July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he go after the party, Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went west to the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to that very serious situation regarding the Croat offensive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've said a couple of things about the Zepa operation and the Main Staff involvement. The Main Staff ordered that attack on Zepa, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say yes when it comes to what was written in the directive; whether there was a specific command, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if I showed you a 10 July order by General Mladic to attack Zepa, would that seem at all odd to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And surely you and the people at the ops room and the operation and training centre in the Main Staff would have been receiving daily and interim combat reports from the Drina Corps on the Zepa operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. One moment, before we proceed to your next question. To the previous question, the witness did answer, but we have no reflection of his answer in the transcript, line 6 of page 7. The question was as follows, Mr. Obradovic: "Well, if I showed you a 10 July order by General Mladic to attack Zepa, would that seem at all odd to you?" What was your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it would not seem odd to me if there is such an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then I ask you about the daily interim reports. You said "yes." And in fact, General Miletic would have been receiving a morning and an evening phone call from the 65th Protection Regiment as you have testified earlier, as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since, as you've already testified, the 65th had elements involved in the Zepa operation, General Miletic would have received information about the 65th's involvement from those phone calls?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that the regiment commander spoke to him about all his subordinated units and their condition on any day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And on the -- that saves a lot of documents that we don't have to go through. And on the 17th, that day that you got there, was General Mladic around Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he was. I reported to my commanding officer upon my arrival, General Miletic, and General Mladic is only the third up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, sir, you're going to know your immediate command chain and, for example, as we know, Mladic has got his helicopter; he takes off to Belgrade; he goes to various battle fronts; and you have told us that when he leaves he put somebody in charge. So when he leaves, you're going to know who is in charge, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He reports to the one he authorises to take over in his stead. He doesn't report to me. I am small fry for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, of course, he doesn't. But you're going to know -- you're going to know if Mladic is around or not. It's a little different environment when Mladic isn't around, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it isn't usual for all subordinated officers to know where their commander is. Sometimes it's -- that's classified information. Sometimes he doesn't want others to know for security reasons and other reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're the chief of operations. You're at the operations room. You would have known where General Mladic was at all times, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You should have known. You would have liked to know. Let's say you would have liked to know, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not that curious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If General Mladic isn't there, General Tolimir is out at Borike, General Milovanovic is out on the western front, who would be the usual people that Mladic would have put in charge? You?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We got that out of the way.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of his assistants to who he gave an oral approval or otherwise authorised them to take over some of the responsibility, but the mere physical absence of the commander from the site does not mean that he sheds his command responsibilities. He -- so his authorities always stay with him, no matter where he is. So wherever he is in the Republika Srpska, he can command from wherever he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We understand that, of course. I'm just going on what you testified in direct examination that when Mladic left, he put somebody in charge. I didn't say "in command." I don't know how it got translated. So --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the assistants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Who's left then? What are our options? You want me to help you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about his assistants, one of the assistants of the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In July 1995, who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistants?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That he would have put in charge?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the morale sector; the head of the mobilization, personnel affairs; the head of the sector for intelligence and security; or the head of the airforce and anti-aircraft defence; or, finally, the head of the administration for planning and development.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I had mentioned to you that -- as we know, that Tolimir is in Borike most of this time period, so let's cut out the head of the intel and security. Of the individuals you've mentioned, who would have been Mladic's most trusted assistant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that General Tolimir was at Borike, which was in the immediate vicinity, and that was a forward command post of the Rogatica Brigade, or it was called the Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. It may have been General Tolimir, and it would be speculation for me to try to establish who was -- who the one was because I had no information, no special information, and he assigned tasks to his assistants; and I, as a chief of department, did not have to know who of his assistants was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question, General, was of General Gvero and the logistics guy and the airforce guy, who is the most trusted by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to a couple of documents. I just want to get your take on a couple of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 192.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as we're getting that, did General Miletic, during July, was he able to pass on orders from his superiors to subordinates?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he able to give orders to subordinates?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were subordinate to General Miletic were the chief of the department for operations and the chief of the department for training. He didn't have other subordinates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let's look at this document that's on the screen, and I think it's a one-pager, so you'll be able to -- you know, I don't -- that screen is hard to deal with sometimes. If I can just give you this so you -- now, this is a document dated 13 July in the name of Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic. We've seen Savcic earlier making a recommendation on -- a very serious recommendation, and this is something similar to that. And we see here that Savcic is passing on to General Mladic and to General Gvero a proposal from General Tolimir about what's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm loathe to interrupt, Your Honour, but prior to the court starting, my client pointed out to me that he was unable to change his monitor from LiveNote to any of the documents, to e-court. A technician came in here, I saw, after, hasn't solved the problem. What I resolved was only to interrupt if a document was put on the screen that related directly to my client. This obviously does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I have decided to interrupt. I think he would like to be able to follow, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Is the situation the same, General Gvero? You still can't see documents on the monitor? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, are you in the same position, or is this a problem only with General Gvero? THE ACCUSED PANDUREVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can see the documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So what I suggest is that for the time being General Gvero moves near, if that's okay with the security officers, and he can follow from there. All right. We've solved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for so organising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, General, that gave you a little chance to take a look at this, but as I was saying, this is Savcic passing on Tolimir's proposal to General Mladic and for information to General Gvero and the commander of the military police battalion of the 65th protection regiment regarding treatment of prisoners of war. And the part I wanted to ask you about is number 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says: "Once the commander of the military police battalion receives this order, he shall contact General Miletic and receive from him additional orders and verify if the proposal has been approved by the commander of the Main Staff." So this document, obviously, anticipates General Miletic giving orders, and he would be giving orders to the commander of the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. In the second part of the sentence, it says: "Verify if the proposal has been approved by the commander of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska." This document is vague. Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic is ordering his battalion commander to report to the chief of the administration for operations and training and to verify whether the proposal put forward by one of the commander's assistants, General Tolimir, has been approved. And yet, he has addressed this document to the assistant for morale who is issuing orders to the commander of the military police battalion. So it's illogical. How can the commander of the regiment have orders issued to him by the commander of the Main Staff, and this is sent to him for his information, and the lower-ranking officer is supposed to verify what the assistant of the commander has ordered, whether it's been approved or not. There is no logic here at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution would disagree with you on that, sir, but perhaps General Tolimir can solve the problem. My question is very simple. Paragraph 4 says that the commander of the military police battalion will receive from him, from General Miletic, additional orders, doesn't it? It's very clear.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this, orders are issued to the commander of the military police battalion by his commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic. Why would his subordinate commander, for whom he is responsible, have orders issued to him by the chief of the administration for operations and training?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think you could ask that question to General Miletic had he issued this order? What do you think would happen to you if when you received this you called General Tolimir and said, General Tolimir, your proposal is -- makes no sense and General Miletic can't order anybody. What do you think Tolimir would say to you about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not a document issued by General Tolimir. It was issued by Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as we've soon before in the document you talked about, Savcic was relied upon to pass on proposals from people. I'm sure that everyone at the Main Staff would rely on the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment who was living with General Tolimir at Borike at the time to pass on if an order for -- or a proposal for General Tolimir. But be that as it may, I think we can leave it at there, and I -- we can go on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 183. And if -- now, this one's very short, but it's still going to be small. So this is a 14 July document. This time, Tolimir has got his actual name at the bottom of it from the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's Rogatica not far from Borike, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Podrinje Brigade had a permanent place in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And that's not far from Borike?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in this document from General Tolimir, we see that he's saying: "In order to monitor activities at Zepa..." I won't go into all of that, but he clearly is telling General Miletic personally that it's necessary to incorporate the Main Staff work plan -- or incorporate the Main Staff and the Drina Corps together in their radio work plans for communication. Why is it that General Tolimir would be directing this specifically to General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Miletic was deputising for General Milovanovic within the staff, and in the organs for arms of service there was Colonel Prole, Lieutenant-Colonel Radakovic, and Major Stojanovic. And they functioned as communications organs. As General Milovanovic was absent, and in the staff General Miletic was deputising for him, then he sent this to him. If I have to comment on the document ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're free to if you want to.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's usual when something is being planned, a combat action, when the plans and preparations are being made to organise communications between the units involved in that combat activity. The combat activities don't begin unless there is a communications plan. This is something unplanned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to try to clarify the translation issue, you told us that General Miletic was -- or that General Miletic was deputising for General Milovanovic. Do you mean standing in for?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer. It was overlapping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, you need to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was replacing him in organising work at the command post, because the organs for arms of service were directly subordinate to General Milovanovic as was the administration for operations and training; and as the senior officer in the staff after the Chief of Staff, General Miletic conveyed tasks and was responsible for discipline and order in that part of the staff where those organs for arms of service were and these communications men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this particular communications issue of -- of coordinating the Drina Corps and Main Staff, that's rather an essential task for the operation of the Zepa battlefield, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communications with the corps existed previously according to the appropriate communications plan; however, this required additional organisation of communications, or the Main Staff had to be asked to organise this for that part of the war theater around Zepa. This is something unusual because usually these communications plans are drawn up before combat activities begin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document. It's 65 ter 2518.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that this is a very important thing, this coordinating communications between the Main Staff and the corps, this job that Miletic is doing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organisation of communications is done by the superior command vis-a-vis their subordinates, and this is done through the communications organ, not through Miletic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I am talking about the document. The job that is referred specifically and personally to Miletic is an important -- this is an important task that he is to do for General Tolimir, isn't it? Or maybe it isn't. Maybe Tolimir just wrote this thing and didn't think it was that big a deal.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wouldn't have written him -- written this had he not considered it important. That was his view of this problem because there is mention here of securing radio apparatus 2K with a cryptographic protection, and the title of the document is "Protection of Secret Military Information." So through the communications organ, means have to be found to be used on the radio communications down there where combat activities are going on in order to prevent leakage of confidential military information, because as you see, it says here: "Protection of Confidential Military Information." And it refers specifically to the KZU 63, which was to be given to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we're going to see some intercepts in a moment, so we'll get a better understanding of how just important radio communications would have been. But I'm more interested in your view, whether this is important, this task. Was it important? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, communications are important for any army, any military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. All right. Looking at this document - let me give you the hard copy - this is a 15 July document and under the name of General Miletic it -- the English is "Chief of Staff representative." It should be, I believe, "standing in for." Just a translation differ. And there is a little handwritten scrawl at the top. I don't know if you can make it out, but our interpreters looking at this have noted that it says: "As promised by Major-General Miletic, 50 MUP men should come from Bijeljina during the night of the 15th and 16th July, 1995." And we see that this is sent to the Drina Corps, and I believe this document came from the Drina Corps archives. So I would suggest that somebody from the Drina Corps received this document and then scrawled that on the top, though you may disagree with me. Now, we see here that, here, General Miletic is reporting on the dispatch of people from your old unit - I think that's your old unit - the 1st Krajina Corps, to help Vinko Pandurevic at the Zvornik Brigade. So what -- what function is General Miletic filling now in, basically, sending troops from one corps to another?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miletic isn't sending this. This is not an order. He's providing information. Probably, this was written based on the commander's decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, I am sure the commander had a role in this, but what is Miletic's role providing this information where he is saying what time the march should start and other directives in here? What role is he -- what function is he fulfilling in the various functions and roles you've been describing for us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's conveying an order from the commander. This is not his decision. The commander can be far away from the ops room. He can be 10, 20 kilometres away, but he can pick up a telephone or go to the command post of a subordinate unit, and say to Miletic, There's a request from such and such a unit for this and this, write an informative document about this. And based on this, he would draw up this sort of -- this sort of note, because this is not an order; this is information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But wouldn't it normally kind of go the other away around that the ops room or someone at the operations department would find out that through the Drina Corps that the Zvornik Brigade needed more help; somebody from operations or somewhere else would make a proposal to General Mladic or whoever was in charge that that person that was in charge -- or excuse me, was in command would then issue the order to send the unit to Zvornik; and then the operations unit would type up this information and send it off to make sure it happened the way the proposal to the commander went and the commander's order reflecting that proposal went? Isn't that the more normal way as opposed to, you know, General Mladic finding out himself and then coming down to the ops room?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sort of request should be sent to the commander. Whether he received it in a written or oral form, I don't know. But if he didn't know whether any unit had available forces, he would ask us whether we knew through following our own forces whether there were forces available. If he knew, he would say, Send this and that from such and such a corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. So the operations department would play a role in this whole process and the eventual sending of this information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We don't make decisions. We only execute the commander's orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you influence the command by making proposals to the commander, don't you, because you know more details then he does?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, there is no room for suggestions or proposals. If he issues an order and says, Do this, he's not asking us for suggestions. He's saying, Write up this and that, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I don't want to argue with you about this, but surely, General Mladic doesn't know whether or not the 1st Krajina Corps can afford to break away one group. That's something that the operations guys that have a view of all the corps are better off to proposing the commander; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. He might have contacted General Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, prior to this and asked him about available forces, because at a certain point, he knew the plan of the corps better than we did in the administration for operations and training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you're not quite there yet. It's still the 15th, so let's not speculate on what he might have done. I was just trying to get the process sorted out. But in looking at that little comment at the top, if this is in fact from a Drina Corps officer receiving this information, this would indicate that someone has spoken to General Miletic and that Miletic has promised MUP units as well. So that would -- would it be normal for the Drina Corps to call the Main Staff and actually speak to Miletic and give an oral indication of their extreme needs on -- for combat reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, General Miletic or the commander of the Main Staff do not have the right to involve units of the police. There is certainly a high-level decision involved here through the Ministry of the Interior and the commander of chief towards the Main Staff to involve these forces. Well, I'm speculating now, but maybe General Miletic had this information, and he said in a conversation, You will receive this, and then this person interpreted this as General Miletic's promise, but he can't promise to give me something that he does not have at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know Mr. Borovcanin, I take it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not especially. I've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we won't get into all the MUP involvement and Kovac's approval with Karadzic and Mladic about supplying MUP units to the Srebrenica area, but I appreciate your comments. I don't think they were speculative. Let's go to another -- let's now go to an intercept that apparently the Muslims heard in the view of the Prosecution, despite General Tolimir's, though it does not have to do with Zepa, so maybe General Tolimir was effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Its' 65 ter 1198. C is the English. B is the B/C/S. And this is just a -- it's a short synopsis that we believe is a Muslim intercept operator writing down a synopsis of something he'd heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It actually sounds a bit like you were just talking about, because if you will see it -- it should come up, but I'll read it to you so you can hear it before you read it. Actually, if you can check out that highlighted one, that'll help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's, I think, on the next page for everyone else in B/C/S. Yes, it's -- you've got to bring it up a little bit. There you go. It's that part on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the synopsis says: "At General Mladic's request, received through Miletic, Colonel Cerovic asked Blagojevic 'all day long' to send some men or a unit. At 2006 hours, Blagojevic reports that five minutes or half an hour ago 50 men left and that he has 60 more down at Kovacevici." So what the Muslims captured, does that make sense to you? Wasn't that what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "I was talking about".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as I read this, it looks like the Muslims overheard Miletic talking to Cerovic saying, Hey, Mladic wants Blagojevic to send men, all day long, somewhere. And then -- well, to Blagojevic. We know Blagojevic is the Bratunac Brigade. We know he sent men up to Zvornik because of the situation Pandurevic was facing. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This says, At General Mladic's request through Miletic, Colonel Cerovic asked Blagojevic. And this, in inverted commas, I think refers to the engagement of these 50 men, so that they were used all day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, this shows Miletic's involvement in this reinforcement process, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but General Mladic is mentioned as preceding that. So it wasn't the decision of General Miletic. It was -- it originated from the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. That's why I said this sounded like your earlier answer.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But Miletic is doing his job?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 3923.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But before we get that, we've heard before -- in this courtroom, and I don't want to go over this with you, but that when a subordinate officer receives an illegal order from a superior, he is duty-bound not to follow it, by JNA, by VRS rules. I am sure you would agree with that. Is it -- what's the situation when, for example, Mladic passes -- wants Miletic to pass on an illegal order? Is Miletic duty-bound to do anything when he receives that illegal order from Mladic to pass on, to say, someone in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The responsibility lies with the one who executes the order, because the rules say the order must be executed in due time and accurately without opposition except when the execution of such an order would be a criminal act or a crime. And in this case, he doesn't have to know what the police will be used for. And the responsibility lies with those who execute the order whether they will do it or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say "police" you mean military police?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This -- the police mentioned here I don't believe is military police. Or -- but it isn't important. The people employed here -- anyway, it says duty to pass this on. This isn't a problem in itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. I did not mean for you to be looking at any document for this question. This is a question that is not meant to have any document, and I'm not suggesting anything about the civilian police in this question. Let me give you a hypothetical. Maybe we can make it clearer. If General Mladic orders General Miletic to order General -- or to pass on his order to Cerovic to steal four buses from the MUP, a criminal act, if -- is General Miletic obliged to pass on this illegal order to the Drina Corps, or is it his duty not to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has to execute it, and if he thinks that's a criminal act, he can turn to the second in command or to the superior officer of the one who issued the order; that is, the commander-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me change the hypothetical. If Mladic says to Miletic, General Miletic, I want men -- I want 500 men in a school killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish the question. Go ahead with the question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Miletic, I want 500 men in a school killed; pass on my order to kill those men to the Drina Corps now. What is the duty of General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you still want to object, Mr. Petrusic, having heard the question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I object. This calls for speculation and is totally unfounded in anything what the Prosecutor is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I put it slightly differently and ask rhetorically through Your Honours, what does it matter what this witness says in relation to this particular issue? It's a matter of legal interpretation of JNA, VRS, and other military rules that my learned friend is asking the witness. And the witness isn't really competent to deal with this, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The -- it's the Prosecution's burden to prove criminal intent, and when they receive an illegal order - I think we have clearly established what that means - what would be in the mind of a trained JNA officer -- what I want to do is see if I can determine credibly what would be in the mind of a trained JNA officer or a VRS officer when he is told to pass on an illegal order because that will help us in our ability to get in the minds of the accused, which is what we have to do when we prove criminal intent. So while yes, under the Geneva Conventions it's your duty, of course, to determine whether we have proven our -- the mens rea of this crime, but I think as getting into what a VRS officer might be thinking when he receives this is potentially important. I mean, clearly, why else did we spend three or four days going over the RS rules if it wasn't to get a feel for what's in their mind? I mean, the RS rules aren't what are at play here. It's the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, by majority vote, Judge Prost dissenting, we agree with the objection raised by Mr. Josse. We don't agree with your objection, Mr. Petrusic, so we move to your next question, please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like us now to see 65 ter number 3923.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is a document, giving the General a hard copy, that is from the Main Staff. We see its from 03-4, which in the operations centre or from the operations unit, dated 21 July 1995. It's very urgent, entitled: "The dispatch of a motorised company from the 16th Krajina to the area of Trnovo." And it's entitled an order, and it's to the command of the Drina Corps and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And as we look at the back of it, standing in for the Chief of Staff, Major-General Radivoje Miletic. And it describes the 16th Krajina Motorised Brigade, and it says that it's been engaged in the composition of the 1st Zvornik infantry brigade in the search of the terrain, the blocking and destruction of crashed Muslim forces from Srebrenica and the wide area of Mount Urdic from 16 to 20 July. And it says: "For the execution of the following task, I order ..." Then it basically looks like it's sending them on to the Trnovo front with some details. Now, sir, this is the same unit that we saw the information document authored by General Miletic that reflected the information of a unit going to the Zvornik Brigade, and now we see this -- they are getting pulled from Zvornik and getting sent to Trnovo, and this is obviously an order, is it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we are now at 21 July - so you're fully active, you're trying, I'm sure, to get caught up with what's going on - we see that this is coming out of your operations room or operations area. Do you remember this, first of all? I know it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you explain, what function is General Miletic fulfilling now as he is, as you've agreed with me, actually issuing an order, "I order ..." and the name of General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. There is a block signature, and it says "SR," and according to the instruction about office -- office operations and archiving, there is no such SR clause. It would be good who -- good to know whose signature this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you. It would be good. But teletypes don't give a signature. So let's take the document at its face, and what function, now, is Miletic fulfilling in issuing this order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he would be the commander. It would be the function of a commander, but he doesn't have that function. We can't take it for granted, as it doesn't bear his signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that came out of the Drina Corps archives. It's stamped, and let's take it as a serious document. And it's simple enough for General Mladic to -- to give General Miletic the authority to issue orders, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be, but then it would -- there would be his signature. I don't know why there is this SR clause. After -- after the name of General Miletic, there is "SR."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I apologise. This did not come from the Drina Corps collection. It came from the RS Brana Luka collection. Sir, you know what "SR" stands for, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the instruction about office operations, which we adhered to. There is no such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know what "SR" stands for, and I can tell you, I don't know who or how many, but people have been testifying in this courtroom about what "SR" means for a long time, VRS guys. So it's not a mystery nor a military secret.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't call it either a mystery or a military secret, but I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It means, according to those witnesses, that the person actually signed it. Anyway, I don't want to argue whether or not this is his signature or whether or not he's become a commander. Let's look at that -- let's look at the second page in the English so anyone can see what it says there, on the English. But surely you would remember if General Miletic, shortly after you getting back to the Main Staff, had the authority to actually issue orders?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In the first paragraph, it actually describes what the job of this Krajina Corps unit had been in Zvornik, searching the terrain, blocking, and the destruction of the crashed Muslim forces. So we can conclude that people in the operations branch actually got a description of what that Krajina corps unit was doing in Zvornik, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's stated here in the preamble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can conclude that you received that information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a question. It was engaged as part of the Zvornik Brigade, and someone had decided to resubordinate it and dispatch it to Trnovo to the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and to report to someone and execute some tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, it's a simple question. Can we conclude that the operations branch at the Main Staff received this particular information about what this unit had been doing in Zvornik, searching the terrain, blocking and destroying the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So the unit that is supposed to change location and the place of the carrying-out of activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. General, in this --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there is no doubt as to the duties of the unit that it had where it was at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, this courtroom has heard evidence that at the time that this Krajina unit was engaged in the terrain in Zvornik, that a unit of soldiers with a patch that said "People from the Krajina" on it, pardon my pronunciation but something like Krajisnici, engaged in a mass execution of some 10 to 15 people. And my question is: If this Krajina unit that's being sent to Trnovo had committed mass murder, 15 people, would the Main Staff have wanted to know about it before sending them off to another battlefront?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question, because I did not have such knowledge then, and I don't have it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question. Would you have -- would the operations branch had wanted that -- would you want that kind was information? Would you want to know that from the Krajina commander, from Vinko Pandurevic, from anybody that had it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether -- or, sorry. I don't understand what you mean when you say "whether we would want to hear it." When I hear of something that happened, then I -- I inquire to learn more. But I must have some initial knowledge that something, indeed, did happen. Then I can inquire to learn more details about whatever happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, it's a simple question. Would the operations unit want to know that a unit that it was assisting and sending to another battlefield, had it been engaged in mass murder? Is that something that you would want to know, or would you just as soon not know and it's okay? I mean, would you want to know that information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I know that something happened, then I would be interested. But that unit that is being dispatched passed nowhere close to us. We had no contact. They only get instructions as to the direction in which they are to proceed to carry out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see it's break time. I have a few rather significant documents and some intercepts, so I would be requesting go over my time limit -- or my time estimate. The witness has gotten into some areas I didn't expect, such as the briefing that was given by Milovanovic, and we have perhaps discussed a little more than I thought we would be discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll resume in 25 minutes' time, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, General Miletic had been standing, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed, in fact. He must have seen me looking at him, but then I saw him sit down, so I imagined he had nothing to say or that he will be speaking to his council now during the break. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Can you give us an estimate of how much longer you will be cross-examining this witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope an hour. Three or four documents and a few intercepts. It really depends on how long, and I will try to keep discussions short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Try to do that. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, General, let's go to 65 ter 2157. I'll give you the document so you can have it. It's -- this is a document I -- you may have had a chance to see this already. The Defence -- it's also 2794. Were you able to see this document in preparation of your testimony in the last couple of days?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this document has been shown to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you've had a chance to study it. My question is about this is: You are obviously there; it's the 21st of July. Do you remember these proposals reaching the operations unit that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They arrived to the attention of General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you do remember them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why would Tolimir be proposing things personally to General Miletic as opposed to Mladic or someone else, like Gvero or Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should be interpreted as a report on the situation in Zepa. In the first three items, the situation in that area is described. In the fourth paragraph, it says, "We believe..." I don't know who but it's in the plural. If General Tolimir was with General Mladic, I don't know why he would be addressing General Miletic as the chief of the administration in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you'll recall, on the same day, the 21st of July, we just saw General Miletic actually issuing orders. So is it a fair interpretation that General Miletic has more authority that day on the 21st than he normally would have, and that is why Tolimir is sending it personally to General Miletic? I mean, you were there. You tell me.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not logical. It's not soldierly. It's outside the chain of command for an assistant commander who is higher up by one step to be subordinated to General Miletic, or for General Miletic to have the role of a superior to General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't there a very simple explanation that General Mladic put General Miletic in charge at the Main Staff that day, and so Tolimir is making proposals to go to the staff so the staff can study them and make their proposals to the commander? Isn't that a fair interpretation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the correct interpretation. I am convinced that General Tolimir would not be happy if the commander were to put General Miletic in a superior position to him, because hierarchy is observed when putting someone in charge and giving him the authority of the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think I might agree with you on that. General Tolimir may not like that, but this doesn't need to be viewed like that, does it? This could be a proposal to General Mladic that's going through General Miletic, the man that's in charge. Not in command, in charge.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me what an aerosol minor bomb is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An aerosol, I know it exists, but we didn't have those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain. I'm not an expert on ammunition, but I assume it has some specific sort of action, some sort of pressure over or below --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've seen a report on the Bihac front where somebody - I'm not even sure which side - launched some sort of projectile, and it came down with a parachute and distributed fuel, and a big explosion goes off. Is that what an aerosol bomb is? The US likes using them in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the staff feel about General Tolimir's proposal to bomb the refugee columns? Excuse me, to -- destroying the refugee columns in order to force the Muslims to surrender? Was that given due consideration by the staff, that last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. They had no comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I believe you said that General Miletic wasn't involved in the negotiations in Zepa in any way, something like that. Am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's what the question was, and I said that to the best of my knowledge he did not participate in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, okay, would he have known about it from his position at the -- at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He might have known about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did he know about it? You were there. It's a big deal. Negotiations with the Muslims in a very historic place, lives at stake, surely you remember whether or not you were involved in it. Did you -- were you aware of the negotiations? Were you kept informed by anybody on the ground about it? Because obviously, if you were, General Miletic would have.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our participation consisted in forwarding information among the persons discussing certain issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were involved, the operations branch?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And unlike the people that are on the ground in the field looking across the table from the enemy, you're able to take the information they provide you, study it, analyse it, and make proposals and ask people's opinions about it, right? The kind of thing you've described that you've -- you and the staff do.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not discuss those negotiations specifically, because the negotiations were conducted somewhere on the ground. If we were ordered to forward something somewhere, then we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recall General Tolimir sending you communiques, making suggestions, making comments, looking for your -- looking for the feedback from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I don't know anything specific about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's see if we can refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 191. This is one of those communiques from General Tolimir, which is, we can see, from the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's dated 25 July, when you were there. It's, again, from the Rogatica Brigade command, noted to be very urgent, to the Main Staff personally, to General Gvero or General Miletic. Now, it's entitled: "Agreement on Disarmament of Zepa." And according to this, the Main Staff has -- in paragraph 1, has received a text of the agreement. And he suggests you send it around to the corps, the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the state commission of war prisoners. It says: "Our representative for exchange of war prisoners cannot make arrangements with the Muslims renouncing the text of the agreement." And then it makes suggestions: "Our commission should demand all our war prisoners, including the ones from Gorazde and Bihac." And then it says: "Advise state commissions." I won't go through all this. And then in number 2, it tells you what the Muslim demands are regarding Gobillard, and it says: "Pass on to UNPROFOR a request to send an office of colonel rank from Sarajevo sector to UNPROFOR checkpoint 2." So it's asking you guys to get in and pass on information. And it's suggesting that Tolimir does not want a General from UNPROFOR, because they don't want a situation like they had in Srebrenica with Morillon. It also says to call ICRC. Now, Tolimir is not just proposing to General Miletic now or General Gvero. He's actually telling them to do this, to do that, talk to this person, talk to that person. Surely, you would have gotten involved in having to do all of those things or some of them, anyway, right? Do you remember it now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. This document is addressed to General Gvero personally or - not "and," but "or" - General Miletic. When it's encrypted and sent to someone personally, then the person in charge of encryption takes it directly to the person to whom the document is addressed. That's why I didn't see this document at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know better than I, but when something comes from Tolimir and it's to one guy or the other, aren't you going to give it to both if they're both there? You're going to make some poor comms guy choose between Gvero and Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir decided to whom the document would be taken when he addressed it, and the comms guy encrypted it, and he can't just give it to anyone but only to the person to whom the document is addressed personally. He takes it to the addressee personally. Here it says: "... either General Gvero or General Miletic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, let's start with Gvero. What in Gvero's position would normally include responding and doing the sorts of things here that Tolimir is asking? Any of this have to do with morale, legal, and religious affairs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to a specific task, and it concerns the disarmament of Zepa. A request is made to contact the state commission for exchanges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I understand, but my question is: What in General Gvero's position would he be involved in this sort of -- these sort of tasks for? Would this be something that would naturally fit within General Gvero's task as assistant commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, exchanges are a legal issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Gvero is a lawyer -- was a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but he had subordinate organs for legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so this could -- given it involves actually an agreement on the disarmament and naturally involved General Gvero's position as the legal guy, legal chief, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first item, it says that General Tolimir is proposing that this agreement be forwarded to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and via that corps to the state commission for the exchange of prisoners of war. Would General Gvero have the need to consult his lawyers or not, I don't know, or would it be sufficient -- would what General Tolimir wrote be sufficient for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm after is, is there -- is this the kind of thing that General Gvero would naturally be doing as the chief legal guy, or is there some suggestion here that General Gvero is the man in charge now and that's why he would -- it would be addressed to him? If you know. You were there is why I -- why I ask you that question. If you know.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't say that because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. General Miletic, what in his position as standing in for Milovanovic on many issues or head of the operations and training branch, do either of those two things suggest that he should be involved in responding to these tasks based on his position?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the persons to whom this is addressed is to pass it on and to act on what General Tolimir asks them to do. It's not for them to make decisions because the agreement has already been made on the ground, so General Gvero and General Miletic don't decide on anything concerning this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't talking about decisions. I was talking about taskings that this is mentioned. I mean, would these taskings be normal for what Miletic was doing at that point, being chief of operations and training and standing in for Milovanovic? Would he be involved in responding to this, is my question.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have to act on this document if it reached him, or he would take it to the commander or ask for the approval of the person who is replacing the commander, deputising for him, and he would inform him, and then he would do what the document asks him to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you remember the -- do you remember seeing this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember making any effort to keep an UNPROFOR general from going to the Zepa area as Tolimir strongly suggests in this? Surely you remember General Smith and his involvement in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Smith was the UNPROFOR commander, if I remember correctly, for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have no recollection of any involvement you may have been in or the operations had been in to try to keep guys like General Smith from showing up in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So neither Tolimir nor Mladic came back to you after this and said, I'd ask you to keep UNPROFOR generals out of this. I hold you responsible for General Smith showing up. He didn't say that to Gvero or Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read just a while ago what it says here, that the situation with General Morillon should not be repeated here. I can't find the paragraph where it says that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Pass on to UNPROFOR a request to send an officer of Colonel rank from Sarajevo Sector to UNPROFOR checkpoint 2 at Boksanica to monitor the execution of the agreement."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. The part I was referring to is the third paragraph under point 2: "Make a note to them that we don't want them to send a General considering that we have information that they want to take advantage of his presence according to similar scenario when they took advantage of the presence of General Morillon in Srebrenica in 1993." And all I was asking, General, is General Smith showed up and kind of mucked up the works a bit, and I imagine Tolimir and Mladic might not have liked that, especially when they told you guys to try to keep that from happening. Does that refresh your recollection? If it doesn't, no problem. We'll go on.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where it says "to prevent."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see the section that mentions Morillon, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it says here: "Pass on to UNPROFOR a request to send an officer of a rank equivalent to Colonel from the Sarajevo sector." And then in the next paragraph, it says: "Make a note to them ..." that is, to UNPROFOR, "... that we don't want them to sent a general considering that we have information that they want to take advantage of his presence according to a similar scenario that was put in place when they took advantage of the presence of General Morillon in Srebrenica." So it doesn't say here "to prevent," but that we should ask that this not be a general but, rather, someone with the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree. Did you do that, or do you know of anybody at the Main Staff that did?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't draw up the request to UNPROFOR. It was Colonel Milos Djurdjic who was in charge of contacts with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this -- so then General Miletic would have been working with Djurdjic on this point?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on just -- you talked a bit about convoys. I'm not going to spend too long with it, but I do want to go over a document or to two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to one you talked about, 5D846.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've got a copy, and you can see that we've -- those are photocopies that you have, and correct me if I'm wrong, but we see this. It's dated 25 November 1994. It's -- this one is to the Drina Corps command from General Mladic. And it's talking about the blockade of four convoys that he had approved. And you went through this for us and talked about it. The one thing I wanted to ask you about is -- it's number 2 of the order, and it talks about: "Organise the necessary preparations for the personnel participating in this task in order to enable them to cope with possible unforeseen steps which may be taken by convoy members." Now, are you at the Main Staff on 25 November 1994? I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I received the order from General Miletic in the second half of November to go to the outward command post to General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, so you -- do you remember this order at all, this thing about this blockade? It's kind --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Do you remember this at all? It comes out of your office.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. 03/4, yes, but I don't remember because I wasn't there on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What I -- I am curious about is this next line. It says: "The blockade" -- in paragraph 2 of the ordered: "The blockade of the convoy must seem as if a subsequent inspection is being carried out because of the convoy's suspicious cargo. Under no circumstances will you indicate that it is a blockade or how long it's going to last. The primary task of our staff is a detailed inspection." Now when he said "it must appear" or "it must seem that this is happening because of suspicious cargo," nowhere does he say that, This thing should be blockaded because of information that you have for suspicious cargo; it's, Isn't this a blockade in order just to search this thing and keep it stalled for some reason.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that here, a detailed inspection requires a longer time for the convoy to stay at these sites. Sometimes the searches would be shorter when there would be no indication of anything suspicious. But if there was intelligence that would require a more detailed inspection, it would -- it would have to stay longer at the inspection point for inspection. And it says here, display a highly professional and correct attitude and an attitude of determination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see that. And I won't stay with this long, sir. It's just this -- isn't Mladic asking the Drina Corps to communicate to the UNPROFOR convoy that they are concerned that this has suspicious cargo and that that's the reason for the blockade, even though they don't have any reason to think that it's suspicious. Because if he did, I'm sure he would have said it in this order. Isn't that what's going on here?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is speculation because the one who issued the order certainly has some informations, and there have been -- there have been goods in some previous convoys, such as ammunition, armaments, and fuel, that clearly exceed the need of an UNPROFOR unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I don't think we -- we need to discuss that anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to 5D884.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I note my version of it has my highlighting and some of my initials on it based on what you did on the screen. It may be easier just to give you my initials or try to get up on the screen what he had done himself, you know, when you were circling initials and things. Maybe that's the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we can get 5D -- and Ms. Stewart will tell me what that is. It got turned into 5DIC00235.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to help refresh your recollection, hopefully you have that with you. I don't know which one it is in your binder. I'm sorry. Maybe Mr. Petrusic could help. But -- there it is. This is one of these requests that was sent by General Nicolai from UNPROFOR, and it was sent -- it was translated by somebody. And you explained that these requests came in through a fax and -- and went to Mladic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you pointed out to us where General Mladic, his initials were. I think that's the -- kind of in that circle with the red 2, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you also pointed out -- I think we need to bring the document -- if we can kick the English off a bit and bring the B/C/S document over, because I think you've showed us that there were some other -- do you see Tolimir's initial on there anywhere?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the right-hand red circle marked with the figure 1. It isn't very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
