utterances.text: Right. And then at the bottom that handwritten part, it refers to -- you think Colonel Djurdjic wrote that as instructions to Captain Novakovic, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you think Novakovic wrote that stuff up at the top about Caura, Domar, Bresa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says informed equals -- or arrow, Caura, Domar, Bresa, and the respective times, 11.35, 11.38, 11.40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we can see, which didn't make the English translation, but we can see that this thing is dated July 1 1995. That's up in the right-hand corner. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do those initials up in the right-hand corner make any sense to you, the ones on top of the date and the ones below it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the -- one of the initials belongs to the man -- to the person who had written "informed Caura, Domar, Bresa."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the captain who is mentioned below.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you think the initials on top of the date are Novakovic. How about underneath the date?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is A/A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's that mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means "ad acta."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means to be archived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And I think you suggested that General Miletic wasn't involved in this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see how this document doesn't indicate his involvement in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, but I think you made a kind of a bigger statement when you testified. Correct me if I'm wrong, but I thought you said he wasn't involved in this process. So tell us now, what -- was General Miletic involved in this in any way, in this convoy process where requests were considered and then decided on and -- and then -- and then communicated to the various parties involved?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, this business is the business of the department of civilian affairs, but based on such decisions of the commander bearing his initials, and sometimes it happened - I don't know why - that sometimes for the sake of speed, we would draft notes that would bear the commander's initials to be passed on to all the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we," you mean the operations branch?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose initials would you prepare?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the commander's initials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who's that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the Main Staff, Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say "we," you mean your branch including General Miletic as the head?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He isn't the head of the department. He's the head of the administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So as head of the administration, General Miletic is involved in this process?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this particular -- we see, General -- what's the chief of assistant commander for intel and security -- what's his interest, or why is he involved in looking this over?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, I don't know. Obviously, these initials preceding the A/A were followed by the initials of General Tolimir. It was subsequently deleted, and then it was written down, and I don't know how exactly that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. We didn't -- we couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Obradovic, the interpreters had a problem with following you. I suggest you repeat your answer entirely. The question was as follows: "Okay, now, this particular -- we see, General -- what's the chief of assistant commander for intelligence and security -- what's his interest, or why is he involved in looking this over?" And you had started by saying: "In this specific case, I don't know. Obviously, these initials preceding the A/A were followed by the initials of General Tolimir ..." Can you continue from there, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, General Tolimir as a chief of section for security and intel, must be acquainted in a way about UNPROFOR requests for the passage of certain convoys from the point of view of security and intelligence assessments. That is his interest. And the -- about the other part, I said specifically about the document being shown on the screen. There is the initials of General Tolimir, and the indication A/A, above those initials on the left. And it seems to me that this indication is crossed out. And to the left of that, there is the commander's instruction or order that -- sorry, not order, "yes." And below that, his initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it clear enough or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Almost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. If you want to proceed with further questions, I think it will help you and us to understand better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The part that's crossed out, what does that say? The part in the middle between the two red circles?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose, I cannot be sure, that General Tolimir put this A/A here and added his initials, and that possibly, subsequently, or probably this document reached the commander - I don't know why - and that he gave his approval by the word "da," "yes," and then added his initials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But crossing out the indication that it should go to archives, what significance is that, if any? Is that any -- AA is what you said, send to archives.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that have significance that either Mladic or Tolimir would have crossed that out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That has no significance. It's up to the commander to decide. General Tolimir could have -- may have had his opinion about this, but the commander's opinion was different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And just in looking at -- I mean, very simply in looking at this, this is a request to have a medical evacuation of three Ukrainian soldiers: a lieutenant, a non-commissioned officer, and a private. So is this a security branch issue when looking at whether this is a legitimate medical evacuation or whether it's some kind of other nefarious thing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was nefarious.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security checks and intelligence checks were routinely done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Tolimir routinely looked at these things.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't claim that. The -- whatever I am saying is my assessment, but I'm identifying whatever is on the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what you're saying is rather serious, and you've just said that security checks were rather routine. So you were in that office every day. I take it you saw these sorts of requests.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally, in my encounters with Djurdjic I saw them. There was nothing unusual about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in these routine security involvement, would the corps security be involved in dealing with convoys for the same reason that Tolimir was interested?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. In the chain of security and intelligence organs, the information would flow from the Main Staff to the lower-ranked elements, depending on the zone of responsibility in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So if it was the Drina Corps zone of responsibility, and there was a security interest by Tolimir in a convoy, you would expect that Popovic would also have -- reflect Tolimir's interest and be interested in that convoy as well? And we don't need to say Popovic. We can say the Drina Corps security.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's normal communication along expert lines between the Main Staff and subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if this convoy gets down to actually a checkpoint, let's say, in Zvornik, in the Zvornik Brigade zone, then it becomes -- then under normal communication along the professional lines, it becomes the responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade security branch, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the security sense. But the command decided about the personnel to conduct the checks at the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I want to go to -- and I want to just, before we leave this document, remind you of the three soldiers from the Ukrainian: Zagichka, Varukha, and Gaspinich. Pardon me for any Ukrainians that I probably offended. Let's keep those names in mind, and now I want to go to 65 ter 2554.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I will -- as we're getting to that, I will remind you - let me give you a hard copy of the B/C/S - that we were looking at some documents yesterday regarding convoys that were signed for General Miletic. What was the name of that fellow that signed for General Miletic? I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At two places, what the Defence attorney asked me, Radoslav Pandzic from the administration for the airforce and anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so that were -- again, I won't get them out, but those were convoy-related documents that were being sent off. Do you remember where they were being sent off to? Those other documents, not this one. I'm sorry. I've forgot.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were like the one before that we had on the screen, before this one. They were faxed requests that came from UNPROFOR, and they were received on the fax of the department of civilian affairs. They were studied by Colonel Djurdjic, Milos Djurdjic, and then he would submit a proposal to the commander, or not, to learn the position of the commander regarding individual requests. Once a commander had perused that, then he would draw up an individual document and send it out to the units that would come in touch with the convoy on its route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so this -- the document that we're talking about, it was sent out to the units that would come in contact with the convoy. That was under the name of General Miletic but signed for him by this guy, Pandzic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably. At the moment he signed it below the block signature of General Miletic, then General Miletic must have been absent. It wasn't his regular duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if General Miletic wouldn't have been absent, he would have been involved in this -- these particular convoy requests signed off by Pandzic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misunderstood me. This was written by Milos Djurdjic, and only signed, because certain documents, notes, information would be signed by General Miletic as the head of the administration. And as General Miletic probably was absent at the time, there are two signatures by this man, Pandzic, who signed it due to Miletic's absence, and Colonel Krsto Djuric, who was probably deployed to the ground to some unit, so there was no officer in charge of ops and training present at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I -- I'm sorry. I shouldn't have asked you about that document without it being on the screen so we could follow it, but let's go on to this particular document that you now have, 65 ter 2554, because it bears the date 1 July 1995, like the previous document we saw from Nicolai requesting medical evac for three Ukrainians. And if we see in paragraph 2 of this document, we see the three Ukrainians. So in this document, it's from the Main Staff, as we see from the first page, and it's to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Drina Corps. And if we go to the end, it's got the block, standing in the for the Chief of Staff, Major-General Miletic. So now we have Miletic involved in this request to the Main Staff by UNPROFOR, and we see several numbers where various things are mentioned, including our number 2, which is clearly the -- that request that we see before. So, I want to ask you about things. Do you see this stamp up in the -- hopefully you've got the one with the stamp in the upper right corner that says "Command of the Zvornik 1st Light Infantry Brigade"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that -- my belief is that means that this was a document that, despite being addressed to the Drina Corps, was sent on to the Zvornik Brigade. And I'd like to take you to number 6. It's page 2 in the B/C/S, and I think it's page -- page 1 of the document that you have. Yes, the B/C/S. Page 2 of the English. And it says: "From Srebrenica to Zagreb, along the same route as the previous item, out on 2 July ..." and I'll skip a bit. It talks about personal equipment and luggage of the personnel that are being rotated, composition of the convoy in both directions, and it lists a Jeep, lorries, 20 people in both directions, cargo in both directions, personal equipment and weapons, rations for their own use, equipment for the vehicles, mail bags, first aid kits, administrative equipment boxes. And then there's a note that is said by General Miletic, and before I get to that note -- I'm sorry, but just -- if we go to the front of this thing, it's number -- it's not 03/4 anymore. It's now 06/18. What is that significance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was registered outside the administration for ops and training, either in the department for civil affairs or, perhaps, in the administration for the airforce, because it's signed by Colonel Pandzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know it's signed by Colonel Pandzic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the lawyer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- showed it to me. The counsel showed it to me during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may assist, I don't think the witness is looking at the right document, because this document is dated the 1st of July, 1995, but I did not show him this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought it referred to this one, because previously there was that fax you asked me about, where I circled that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you were shown was the request by UNPROFOR that got faxed and circled by Mladic and Tolimir. Now what I'm showing you is the communication sent out by Miletic that included the information in that fax. There is no indication -- the only indication of the author of this document is at the end of the document, and it's Radoje -- Radivoje Miletic, correct? This is a document, sir, you have not seen. And I know it's late, and we'll be done soon.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, Your Honours, to explain. I have no bad intentions here, but when the counsel showed me a set of these faxes when putting his questions, there was a document, which had the same form as this, more or less, and there was a signature there, which I identified. I thought this was the same document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Completely understandable. There has been a lot of documents. This is a new one. So take a look at it, especially at the end of it. I don't think he showed you this one. This one's related to the ones that he showed you, but it's not one that he showed you apparently. It's just Miletic's name on this one. Those other ones were from --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- a long time ago. Okay. So let's see what Miletic has to say in this note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you proceed. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we ask the witness to please take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you remove your headphones, please, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is going too far, Your Honours, and misleading the witness. We can't mix various things that aren't similar. This document, we only see the block, the signature. It's just a copy. The document that we submitted were those that we came by. They were the originals. So I don't think that the Prosecutor can draw a parallel between these documents as he has just done. We don't know who actually signed this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Madam. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an interesting argument. However, this document is directly related to that other document, because as we can see the three uniquely named and numbered Ukrainian soldiers are on this document. And what we have here is -- is very simple. We have the UN request saying, Please let these three Ukrainian soldiers go out. Mladic looks at it, Tolimir looks at it or vice versa, and then what happens with it is communications get sent back to UNPROFOR saying yay or nay, and communications, as the witness said, get sent back to the corps that it's going through. What counsel did not show you in direct examination is what I am showing you now, is the communique from the Main Staff under Miletic's name to the Drina Corps saying that these have been approved or disapproved. And what we're seeing now is a little note about a Srebrenica convoy that Miletic is writing to the Drina Corps to make sure they get his instructions right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's no confusion here. You know, she can argue that this is not a valid document because of whatever. I don't know if we have the original or not. I think we do because this particular document, as I said earlier, I believe came from the Zvornik Brigade collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would simply like to make things as clear as possible, and we can then expedite matters. We have not challenged that documents addressed to the units came from the staff with this block signature of General Miletic. What we are challenging is how the Prosecution is proceeding now and whether or not these documents actually bear his name or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to respond to that, if I could, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Defence specifically -- they had this document. This is not something we're holding back, the one I'm using now. They, I must believe, specifically chose not to show the witness this document, the -- if you will, the final piece of the puzzle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Because we are -- it's going to be ping-pong and -- stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I cannot just stop here. I am really sorry, but this is an insinuation that is really not relevant. We submitted to the witness documents that are very similar to this one. Why would we not have shown him this one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So our unanimous decision is that we see nothing irregular in the way the Prosecution is proceeding, so we are allowing the question and the use of the document. We also want to just encourage you to avoid resorting to what we had told you is certainly not our preference. If there is one counsel who is dealing with a witness, please try to avoid having the second one, et cetera. We allowed it recently in one or two occasions, but if possible, please try to avoid it as much a possible. I do understand that sometimes there is an urgent need to intervene, and one does pop up and interject. However, try to limit it as much as you can, please. All right. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And for everyone's knowledge, this document that I have right now, 65 ter 2554, is in evidence. It came in through Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want to read this note, page 3 in English, page 2 in the B/C/S. It says: "The movement of the convoys under items 5 and 6 above, which has been approved conditionally, should be specially controlled by teams at checkpoints and liaison officers of the Drina Corps command before they enter the territory of Republika Srpska on their return from Zagreb. Check the cargo in the six lorries. It has been agreed that the six lorries will transport humanitarian aid for Zvornik, and the same number of lorries should bring humanitarian aid to Sarajevo, Sarajevo Muslims. "If the lorries come to Zvornik without the said cargo, do not let them go to Sarajevo or Srebrenica." And it continues: "In other words, when the convoy arrives in Zvornik, check it, establish what it is carrying, and inform the commander, after which instructions regarding continuation of their journey will be given. Inform about this only the men who deal with such issues and use the details for internal purposes only. Do not reveal them to third persons." Now, this very clear note that goes out under the name of General Miletic -- so isn't it the duty of the person sending out this communique to the Drina Corps and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to clearly explain the orders of the commander so that the guys in the corps and on the ground at the checkpoint understand precisely what is excepted of them by the commander? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this information leading to the drawing up of the standpoint had to arrive either from the commander or from the organs who had at their disposal more information concerning the movements of UNPROFOR. I think that here Miletic wrote what somebody demanded that he write and that he sent this information to the Sarajevo Romanija and the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you, and that is what my question was about. Isn't it General Miletic's duty, when he gets this order, to be able to put it in a language that the guys that receive it down the line can clearly understand?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the main points were given to him either by the commander or someone who had this information. Most probably, it was the commander because this contains orders as well. In fact, it draws attention to procedures that were already in place pursuant to previous orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can tell from this detailed instruction that General Miletic knows what he's talking about. He knows about this process, and he knows how to communicate to these guys, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, following his orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can we -- is it also correct that it's General Miletic's job to advise General Mladic on these sorts of issues, to help him understand the bigger and more detailed picture and to provide proposals for General Mladic so that when General Mladic issues an order like this, he does it so knowingly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically in this case, this is information probably coming from intelligence security organs rather than operations organs. Based on the information given to the commander, the commander gave instructions to Miletic as to how he should draw this up and how he should draw attention to the procedure at certain points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will go back to my question. Generally, for General Miletic to know about these issues and for General Mladic to know about these issues, General Miletic would be providing proposals and information so that General Mladic can make the best decision possible, correct, regarding convoys?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has answered this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't believe he has, and I -- in cross-examination, even if he had, I think there's -- it's not a proper objection, but he hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, anyway, because we are wasting more time like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't that true that in issues that we see General Miletic -- we've seen many, many of these sorts of convoy documents going down to the corps under Miletic's name. Isn't it important for Miletic to provide the commander with information about these convoys and make proposals regarding the convoys so that the commander can make the best decision possible?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the organisation of the command of the Main Staff is such that all lower-level organs serve the command, and each one submits to the commander the relevant information that can help him make decisions. But this information is not information from the relevant administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This information about convoys would be coming from General Miletic and his experience with convoy documents. There is many, many of them that he's been involved in. So isn't it true that General Miletic advised the commander about issues related to convoys?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're wrong. Miletic figures here only as the signatory of a document, because the person dealing with these activities does not have the right to sign this type of information. And this is based on instructions or orders coming from the commander which could be issued orally or conveyed through Djurdjic to compile this and draw up a document containing the decisions made by the commander concerning each one of these convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll try one more time. I'm not talking specifically about this document. You've already told us that Tolimir got involved in this, and perhaps the order came right from Tolimir or the proposal to Mladic came right from Tolimir and than got fed down to Miletic, and it was just Miletic's job to communicate it in the best way possible. I'm talking about generally. We see General Miletic drafting material and sending it off to the Drina Corps over and over again with these sorts of detailed explanations about what to check, what not to check. And my question is, General, given that Miletic is sending all this communication and this detailed information about convoys, can't we conclude that he is in a position to advise the command about convoys?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer that question. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is the same as before. The witness has answered this several times regarding procedure, the procedure for the approval and passage of convoys, both in general and in specific instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in a way you are right, but again, we are in cross-examination so -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'll try to make it simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you insist on this question or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can go after it in one more way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you insisting, General, that despite we see many, many documents going out under General Miletic's name to Drina Corps and to UNPROFOR, for that matter, that despite his clear involvement in communicating to the corps that are involved with these convoys, and despite his knowledge in this area, he plays no role whatsoever in advising the command on convoy issues; is that what you're saying? Yes or no, and you can explain.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer in this way. General Miletic doesn't have to be with a commander when a decision is taken. Certain faxes and requests are involved, and it's Colonel Djurdjic who is with the commander in that case, who the commander will consult, whether this one or that one, but the commander will give detailed instructions about every convoy, and Colonel Djurdjic will draw up the document and bring it to General Miletic for his signature. He doesn't want to tire the commander with this or bother him with this because the commander has already made the decision. I think I've been clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I think we understand. One more convoy document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 3924. And -- and we don't have an English translation of this, so, you know, I will try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we have here, General, is a 31 March 1995, and we have a -- a document under the name of Milovanovic, and it's to the command of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo. And my understanding is that it's just a list of a bunch of convoy requests and whether they're approved or not. Is that correct? Just roughly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are 14 ordinal numbers here with the numbers of the convoys and their routes, and there is a request being sent to the Main Staff for its approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we blow up this stamp quite a bit? Just if we could get the stamp centred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General, I am going to hand you -- I'm going to hand you this original of the document that we have so you can look at it, because it's the original stamp. And I want to first of all ask you, do you see a "za" written down there? It unfortunately to be like its underneath the -- what's written down is -- I think it's "Vojske," that word on the left. Do you see the "za" in there when you look at the original?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In handwriting, you mean? Handwritten?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to look at the handwritten part yet. I'm asking you, can you find the "za"? I mean, I -- it's -- there can be writing that can be seen both in the blow-up and in the [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the letter V and J, where it says "Vojske," the Main Staff of the army, Voskje, there is something there, and it might be "za" between the letter "O" and the "J" in the word "Vojske" or "army."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're right, Vojske. Can you make out the original? Can you see that same thing in the original? Do you see the -- what looks like a "z"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Same place in the original, on Vojske. It's always best to look at the original. If you can't make it out, don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see -- the same thing you saw on the screen, do you see it in the original, that little squiggle?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it look like a "za" to you on the original?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can discern it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that signature, that's not Milovanovic's signature, is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic's. And he was authorised by the Chief of Staff to sign these informative documents. We inform you that we have not approved, but it's the commander who did not prove, not the signatory of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. We got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if I can just -- another question or two on this topic, then I think we'll be done with convoys with just a little bit more to go, Your Honour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's time for the break. I think -- how much more?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe 20 minutes on a few intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then we'll have the break. No, I ask you because if you were talking of five minutes, then we would have continued for five minutes and then had the break afterwards. But we'll have the break now, 25 minutes, and please try to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we go to 65 ter 2554. I apologise. We had this on the -- we've talked about this briefly, but I -- in my haste I forgot an important part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I could ask you to look at the screen on this one. This is the document that was sent in Miletic's name to -- and that was received by the Zvornik Brigade that we see it went to the corps, and then the corps must have sent it on to the Zvornik Brigade. And if we see the B/C/S version, it says, "security organ" handwritten on it. So, General, if that was handwritten by a person that received this from the Zvornik Brigade command, what does that mean? Well, I can simplify it. It means that the security organ ought to see this document, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know whether that was written at the command of the Drina Corps or down at the brigade level, but obviously somebody wrote on this that it should go to the security organ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, since, you know, handwritten stuff wouldn't come through on a teletype, I believe this is the Zvornik Brigade, but we'll check on that. That's a good point. And then just going, again, briefly to page 3 in the English, page 2 of the B/C/S. When General Miletic is explaining in this middle paragraph under "note," and it's in part six, the end of part six: "In other words, when the convoy arrives in Zvornik, check it, establish what it's carrying, and inform the commander..." That would be the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If in the letterhead of the document it says Main Staff, then the chief of Main Staff should be informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't think based on the context of this that they would -- that this has to do with the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If the document was sent from the Main Staff, then the chief of Main Staff is met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it was -- let's assume it was sent by the Drina Corps to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the lines of information --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. This was too fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, you went a little too fast for the interpreters. You need to answer it again, slowly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, as you said, the command -- this came from the Zvornik Brigade, then the commander of the Zvornik Brigade will inform the commander of the Drina Corps of this, and the commander of the Drina Corps will inform the chief of Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understood. And can you give us your opinion when it -- the next line down it says: "Inform about this only the men who deal with such issues." Who does that mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons are meant who are involved in the cooperation with UNPROFOR and with the passage of convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that include, in your view, the security officer of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to this, no, but if we read the note on the document of the Drina Corps or the Zvornik Brigade, we could infer that. But we cannot make that conclusion based on this note you referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we can suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's not suppose. We'll be through soon, especially if we don't suppose too much. Okay. Let's go back to 65 ter 3924, and I'll give you that original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there is a problem with translation. I think there is a mistake in the transcript. I am not sure if it's the transcript or interpretation, but at page 66, line 3, I don't think that the witness spoke about the head of the staff. I think he spoke about the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll -- we'll put it -- thank you, Madam Fauveau. We'll put it to the witness. You were asked a question by Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Obradovic. The question was: "Let's assume it was sent by the Drina Corps to the Zvornik Brigade." And you said: "If, as you said, the command -- this came from the Zvornik Brigade, then the commander of the Zvornik Brigade will inform the commander of the Drina Corps of this, and the commander of the Drina Corps will inform ..." who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the Main Staff. Your Honours, it's the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the way I understood it, as well, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about line 12?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Line 12 of page 66?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 65. Yes. And again, you were asked -- it was pointed out to you, and when General Miletic is explaining in this middle paragraph under "note," and it's in part 6 -- the end of part 6: "In other words, when the convoy arrives in Zvornik, check it, establish what it's carrying, and inform the commander..." That would be the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, right? And your answer, according to the transcript, says as follows: "If in the letterhead of the document it says 'Main Staff,' then the chief of Main Staff should be informed." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. If the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska is mentioned in the letterhead, then this refers to the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That was an important thing to make clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. General, you -- if you could take what we have here as -- like we've before -- is this is the letter, looks like, from the Main Staff to UNPROFOR with Miletic signing for Milovanovic, just approving or disproving many convoys, and you have the original as we found it stapled together with several requests from General Nicolai. And so, like you did for the Defence, and I think we can go through this pretty quickly, could you just take a look at those individually? I'm not so interested in the content, but what is important to point out here that does not come through on the screen, and I think you will agree with me, is that sometimes we see blackouts on the UNPROFOR document, which is a traditional thing UNPROFOR might do. Other times we see what is blue ink underlining particular points on these UNPROFOR requests, and other times we -- it looks like some kind of a weird green highlighter that's used. So if you could just flip through all of those to confirm what I'm saying, to say if you see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just for the record, the initials that we see there on the original are in black pen. The underlines and the highlight -- the underlines are in blue, and the highlighting is in this green colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we see anything that the Prosecutor is referring to, these annexes to this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, and Mr. Petrusic, I had shown the original to Mr. Petrusic at the break so he could see the green and the blue and the black and the way it was attached. So that's what we're referring to. He may not have known that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy, are you satisfied with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not the problem, Mr. President. I have seen these documents, but none of the accused have them, especially not our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These have all been disclosed, and I have no objection to the accused looking at the original if they want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed along those lines. Can we have them put either on the ELMO or given to the accused to see straightaway, particularly General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honours, you may want to just -- the General is about to agree with me that he saw blue lines, he saw green, and he saw black initials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct, General?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell one colour from another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We just got to get it for the record, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could just show that -- if we could show the original documents, well, certainly to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- but the ELMO won't reflect the colours. That's the only problem that there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We could go to the first page, the next page over. This is a cover letter, which is obviously a Main Staff document, and it's a cover letter to -- that's stapled on to UNPROFOR document in B/C/S, as everybody will see. If we could go to the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Show them quickly to General Miletic because it's more of concern to him than --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page on e-court. THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] I think it is more important for the judges to see this. I've seen it long ago, and what follows is more important than the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with the General on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we look on the E-court of the first page, you can see the problem because you can't tell the difference between the colours and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We might try the ELMO as the General looks over it, and I just want to -- could we see the -- try to get it so the full document is on the ELMO. We don't have the top. We don't have the initials. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, that's -- it's a "no" circled, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose initials are those next to it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initials of the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And to try to save some time, I think we see General Mladic's initials on each one of these pages with either a "no" circled or some --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on ERN 8413, we have a "za" crossed out and a "no" circled with General Mladic's initials again. And that's page 9 in e-court, but -- oh, you just went by it. Okay. There is an example of the "za" -- sorry, the "da," "yes," being crossed out, and does that mean that Mladic crossed that out and put in "no"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who dealt with this document, probably Colonel Djurdjic as this is within his purview, wrote "yes/limitation," and he crossed out in black -- actually, no, not he but the commander crossed out this in black because you can see his initials, and it says "no."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So we can tell from this that there is somebody - probably, you believe, Djurdjic - going through this, underlining, highlighting, doing various things, making his recommendation, and Mladic is either confirming it or changing it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer. It wasn't audible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. They didn't hear your answer to my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. And on the basis of everything here, Djurdjic signed all these requests and wrote up there: "We inform you that we have not approved the following convoys ..." and then he took this to General Miletic for his signature so that this notification could be sent to UNPROFOR, and the decision was made by the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General, and just -- that should be, hopefully, finished with that. There are packets -- just for the Court's knowledge and the Defence, there are packets like this in the original format where convoys have been approved as well. I chose that particular group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go to some intercept conversations that I want to ask you about. The Muslims, it is our case, were able to, despite General Tolimir's request for encryption, intercept some communications; and let's -- the first one we could go to is 65 ter 1231 A in the English and 1231 B in the B/C/S. The copy I have, General, is handwritten. I don't know if you can make much of it, but I will read what I think is a reliable transcription of that. Actually, I don't need to read it all, but this is a conversation that we're told happened on the 17th of July at about 1950 hours. So I think you were -- you should have been at the command post about that time, and it was between General Krstic and General Mladic. Do you know -- you've probably been asked this, but I'm sorry, I don't remember. Did you see Mladic that first day you got to Crna Rijeka, or do you know if he was there? And he would have been, you know, talking on the telephone over the radio.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at the command post or in the area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, according to this, he should have likely been at the command post, and this is between a person named Krstic and Mladic, and you can see here that Mladic refers to Krstic as Krle. Do you know that that is a nickname of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when Krstic confirms that Mladic can hear him, Mladic says: "Full steam ahead." Krstic says: "Understood." Mladic says: "Get in touch with Miletic on a secure line. Full steam ahead. I didn't accept the Turks' conditions." And then Krstic: "Understood." And then Mladic: "Keep up the work. Bye." Krstic: "Roger." And I'm sure you know at the time General Krstic is leading the operation on Zepa and that the Muslims, you may recall, had certain conditions during the negotiations at about this time, and that -- I think it's a historical fact that Mladic didn't accept the initial conditions. So given if this is true, what I have said, why -- in the process or in the organisational sense, why would Mladic want Krstic to tell Miletic full steam ahead? Why is it important for Miletic to know that Mladic has decided to go forward with this Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps you're misinterpreting this. This was communicated on an open line, because the Muslim side intercepted it, but it may be assumed that General Mladic gave some instructions to Miletic which he would convey to Krstic, but not on an open line in order the protect the information. That's why he's telling him to call up General Miletic using a protected line so that Miletic could inform him of the commander's decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, and I agree with you on that. I think that's what's happening that General Mladic wants Krstic to get in touch with Miletic on the secure line to inform him of the commander's decision. But why does -- why would Mladic want the chief of operations in training, the guy that's standing in for Milovanovic, why would he want Krstic to inform him, Miletic, of Mladic's intentions? Just -- why does the chief of operations or a person in his situation need to know this militarily? That's my question, a simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is no foundation for this question. The witness is being called on to speculate once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, the witness is there at the time. Second of all, the witness has agreed with me about the clear meaning of this, as far as I understood his explanation. And so if that is the meaning of it - be this the fact of this intercept or it can viewed as a hypothetical, so we don't have decide whether it's true - it's still an important question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't see any room for speculation here. It's a straightforward question, which the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, General Mladic said, on a non-secure line: "Full steam ahead." This is probably his approval for the task that Krstic received either from him or from somebody else, in fact, for the combat activities. And when he says: "Contact Miletic on the secure line. Full steam ahead. I didn't accept the Turks' conditions...", probably Krstic is to receive some information which should not be heard by the other side, something that General Mladic conveyed to Miletic to pass on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General, and I agree with that, but why is it important for Miletic to know this information as opposed to Gvero or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What information is the Prosecutor referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The information that was referred to in the previous question on page 74, if I understand it well. If I am not reading you well, Mr. McCloskey, then please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the General and I agree on the meaning of this, and I'll try to set the scene a little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But General, you're back. It's the third day of operations for Zepa, one of the key enclaves in Directive 7. It's a very difficult battle at this point. Men are dying. There is an operations room. The operations guys are there. I'm sure Miletic is there. There's a negotiation going on. It falls through. Mladic says: "Full steam ahead." Why does guy that's the head of the operation centre, the chief of operations, probably standing in for Milovanovic, why militarily does Miletic need to have -- to know this? It's a simple question. My guess is you were in that operation room or were unpacking.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miletic was at the command post. We don't know what he's supposed to pass on to Krstic when he calls General Miletic, but it's evident from this that Krstic was supposed to get in touch with General Miletic on the secure line, for him to pass on to him something from the commander that was not supposed to be heard on a non-secure line. It had to do with combat activities, and it had to be secure so that the intentions of the forces of our side would not be known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have information that in the English transcript it's not clear who is passing information on to whom and who is supposed to get in contact with whom, Krstic to Miletic or Miletic to Krstic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which part of the transcript, in particular, are you referring to? Which lines? Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] [In English] For him to pass on to him something from the commander. It is not clear who is him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure we need to clear that up. The document's been specific. The witness has been specific three or four times, so it speaks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think it's clear enough as well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, General Miletic as the chief of operations and training, as the guy in charge of the command centre, would really need to know that Mladic has gone forward with the Zepa attack, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Administration, the administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Administration. But the chief of operations and training administration really needs to know that General Mladic has decided to go forward with the Zepa operation because he is, as -- in your words, following the combat and is at the head of the command centre, which is the information hub and is a critical part of the combat, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm truly sorry to intervene again, even though I know this is not what you wish. But it's exactly what I said. The questions of the Prosecutor are completely opposed to the answer given by the witness. I think it's absolutely not clear with what the witness actually said with regard to who had to pass on information to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to this. This is this communicating that we've seen before, and it's really late in the day for this to be going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we have already stated that we -- in our minds, having read the transcripts, all the questions that have been put for the last ten minutes, there is no doubt as to what the witness has been saying. So...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but you can make a submission later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript does not reflect what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but then that is something different. If you think that the transcript does not reflect what the witness has said, we'll ask the witness to remove his headphones - please remove your headphones - and you tell us where it doesn't reflect what the witness has stated. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness said is that General Krstic was supposed to call General Miletic to obtain some information from General Miletic, and the Prosecutor constantly refers to information that Krstic conveyed to Miletic, but it's exactly the opposite that was said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's an argument, and it's not true. I have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave it at that. That's -- if you read the last two, three pages, I don't know where you're getting this from, Ms. Fauveau. So let's ask the witness to put his headphones once more and proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'll try one more time. When General Mladic wants information communicated to General Miletic by General Krstic, we can conclude, can't we, that General Miletic is an important part of the communications chain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had the role that is envisaged for him in the establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is your answer yes or no? Is he an important person in the information chain regarding this ongoing operation in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "Get in touch with Miletic." He is not saying who will transmit what to whom. He's just saying: "Get in touch with Miletic on a secure line..." and then he says to Krstic: "Full steam ahead. I didn't accept the Turks' conditions." So he's informing Krstic that he has rejected the conditions, he's ordering him to go ahead at full steam, and he's ordering him to get in touch with Miletic. But who will say -- give information to whom, that's not clear from this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I surrender. Let's go on to the next intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 1237 B in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if you look at -- there's a series of them, but it's the one that starts at 1954 hours. This is a conversation between Tolimir and an X, and a simple question about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could check the page, intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, that's not the right one. I apologise. 65 ter 1237. It's at 1954 hours. 1327, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you see the one I'm talking about, right, 1954 hours, while we're waiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we -- for the English translation, can we move it over so we can see if there's the X and the Ts? There we go. That's important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This conversation is alleged to be between Tolimir and a person identified as X, and X tells Tolimir, near the end of this, that: "You're fully replacing me in the command." This is 24 July. I think we can all figure out if someone said "You're fully replacing me in the command" to Tolimir, that would have had to have been Mladic. Do you remember that on 24 July that Mladic told Tolimir that he was going to be the guy in charge at the command? It sounds a lot like what you said earlier. When Mladic is out, he puts somebody in charge.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the content, who might tell Tolimir he would be replacing him? Who could Tolimir be replacing him? Judging by the imperative, by the hierarchy, it could have been the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, who said: "You're fully replacing me in the command," but he emphasizes "in the command."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And that's kind of what -- that's similar to what you'd said the other day, that when Mladic left he would put somebody in charge at the command. My question is, you were around there then. Do you remember that happening?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that because I don't know where Tolimir was or where Person X was when this conversation was conducted. This doesn't mean that Tolimir was in my presence or I in his, for me to say that I heard this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm just asking you if you remembered Mladic doing this, and if you don't, you don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 1395, A, and in the B/C/S, B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, General, this -- don't look at the part that's crossed out. It starts the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to finish within the next two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I -- yes, I would really like to finish. I will finish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This -- I want to remind you that on August 2nd, there were -- you may recall there were 500 to a thousand, at least, able-bodied Muslim men fleeing the Zepa area going across the river into Serbia, and I just -- my question is: Do you remember that situation? It would have been a hot topic at the ops room at the time.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that this happened, but I don't know -- or I don't recall whether it was the headline news on the television news broadcast, but we got this information through the daily combat reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't remember getting a report from Beara to Miletic about this situation like it says in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's to 65 ter 3911.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many more questions do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I've got two intercepts and two questions. They both involve this -- this person, according to the Muslims. They involve General Obradovic. They should be quick. I know we don't like to keep the other Court waiting, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not only that. Ms. Fauveau -- or Mr. Petrusic, do you have a redirect, as well, which I suppose you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then we will have to continue tomorrow. Thank you. Mr. Obradovic, I'm afraid we didn't manage to finish. Perhaps you could help yourself a little bit better if you kept your answers shorter. We'll reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.
